operations.scenario: A strategist compares two failed launches in unrelated industries. Instead of cataloging what each team did wrong, she proposes that both failed because decision-makers received corrective signals only after commitments became irreversible.
operations.explain: The strategist maps a shared relational structure across otherwise different cases. That is analogical reasoning, and it may support a more general causal hypothesis.
operations.contrast: Causal analysis is involved in the proposed explanation, but the distinctive move is aligning two cases by a shared structure. Decomposition would separate either launch into parts.

operations.scenario: A consultant has been asked to improve a client’s onboarding emails. After examining the request, he changes the working question from “Which emails should we rewrite?” to “At which point do new customers become uncertain about what to do next?”
operations.explain: He changes the problem representation and the question guiding the investigation. That is problem reformulation.
operations.contrast: Diagnosis would determine the cause of observed difficulty; synthesis would combine insights into a coherent whole. Neither is the defining move yet.

operations.scenario: A researcher sees three plausible explanations for an unexpected behavior. She asks which explanation would make the observations least surprising and identifies what additional evidence would distinguish it from the alternatives.
operations.explain: She reasons toward the best available explanation from incomplete observations: abductive inference. The proposal remains provisional.
operations.contrast: Deduction derives implications from premises; classification assigns an item to a category.
operations.tell: which explanation would make the observations least surprising

operations.scenario: An analyst takes a complicated governance framework and separates its decision rights, escalation paths, accountability rules, and review cycles so that each can be examined independently.
operations.explain: The framework is divided into analytically useful constituent aspects. That is decomposition.
operations.contrast: Abstraction could follow if the analyst constructs a selective representation, but separating the parts is the action described.
operations.tell: so that each can be examined independently

operations.scenario: A designer studies a neighborhood association, a distributed software team, and a volunteer network. She represents all three as nodes connected by information flows and decision rights, ignoring their domain-specific labels.
operations.explain: She constructs a selective, domain-independent representation that preserves relational structure. That is abstraction.
operations.contrast: Extraction would retrieve information already present; evaluation would judge against criteria.

operations.scenario: A manager has observed the same bottleneck in four monthly cycles. She concludes it may recur next month, but explicitly notes that the prediction is uncertain because the staffing model recently changed.
operations.explain: She infers a likely pattern beyond the observed cases, while recognizing uncertainty. That is inductive inference.
operations.contrast: Deduction would establish a conclusion from premises; problem reformulation would change the governing question.
operations.tell: She concludes it may recur next month

operations.scenario: Two competing proposals both address customer confusion. An advisor establishes criteria for feasibility, likely impact, and evidence quality, then compares the proposals against those criteria before recommending one.
operations.explain: She judges alternatives against explicit criteria to reach a decision: evaluation.
operations.contrast: Synthesis would integrate elements into a combined whole; abstraction would change the representation by preserving selected properties.
operations.tell: compares the proposals against those criteria

operations.scenario: An engineer knows that a system slows when one component becomes overloaded. Rather than accept the explanation, she traces the sequence of events and checks which interactions could actually produce the observed delay.
operations.explain: She investigates the interacting processes that could generate the outcome. This is mechanistic analysis.
operations.contrast: Analogical reasoning compares relational structures across cases; generalization extends a claim beyond observed instances.
operations.tell: checks which interactions could actually produce the observed delay

operations.scenario: A writer has several separate observations about a community’s objections to a policy. She integrates them into one coherent account showing how incentives, identity, and perceived fairness reinforce one another.
operations.explain: She integrates distinct insights into a coherent explanatory account, which is synthesis.
operations.contrast: Classification sorts observations; extraction isolates information without constructing the integrated account.
operations.tell: integrates them into one coherent account

operations.scenario: An operations lead reads a lengthy incident report and isolates the exact timestamps, error codes, and affected services without changing their meaning or grouping them into a new explanatory structure.
operations.explain: She retrieves specific information already present in the source. That is extraction.
operations.contrast: Abstraction would construct a selective representation; diagnosis would identify the nature or cause of a problem.

operations.scenario: A product owner notices that teams use the word “ready” inconsistently. She defines a precise boundary between work that meets the entry criteria and work that still requires discovery.
operations.explain: She establishes a conceptual boundary and criteria for category membership: conceptual delineation.
operations.contrast: Causal analysis would investigate influences; analogy would compare structures across cases.

operations.scenario: An investigator sees that a campaign’s results declined. She examines several possible sources of failure, checks the evidence for each, and determines that the tracking implementation, rather than the message, is responsible.

operations.contrast: Abstraction changes representation; synthesis integrates findings.

operations.name: Abstraction
operations.definition: Constructing a selective representation that preserves relevant properties or relationships while setting aside others.
operations.distinction: Extraction retrieves information; abstraction changes how it is represented.
operations.trigger: Current representation is too detailed, domain-bound, or poorly suited to the objective.

operations.name: Decomposition
operations.definition: Separating a whole into meaningful parts, dimensions, or stages for examination.
operations.distinction: Abstraction changes representation; decomposition partitions.
operations.trigger: The whole is too complex to reason about at once.

operations.name: Temporal decomposition
operations.definition: Dividing a process or development into meaningful time-based stages.
operations.distinction: A temporal lens plus decomposition; it may also use abstraction.
operations.trigger: You need to inspect change, transitions, or phases.

operations.name: Causal analysis
operations.definition: Examining relationships of influence, mechanisms, and conditions that produce effects.
operations.distinction: Diagnosis identifies a particular problem or fault; causal analysis can be broader.
operations.trigger: The objective is to understand why an outcome occurs.

operations.name: Diagnosis
operations.definition: Identifying the nature or cause of a specific problem through discriminating evidence.
operations.distinction: Abduction may propose candidates; diagnosis tests them.
operations.trigger: Something is wrong and competing causes are plausible.

operations.name: Abductive inference
operations.definition: Proposing the most plausible explanation for observations while acknowledging alternatives.
operations.distinction: Deduction derives implications; induction extends patterns.
operations.trigger: You have incomplete evidence and need explanatory hypotheses.

operations.name: Inductive inference
operations.definition: Inferring a broader probable claim from observed instances.
operations.distinction: A conclusion is not guaranteed by its premises.
operations.trigger: You see repeated cases and want a cautious general claim.

operations.name: Deductive reasoning
operations.definition: Deriving what follows logically from premises or assumed rules.
operations.distinction: Soundness depends on premises as well as valid reasoning.
operations.trigger: You want implications, predictions, or consistency checks.

operations.name: Analogical reasoning
operations.definition: Mapping corresponding relationships between different cases or domains.
operations.distinction: Similarity of surface features alone is weak evidence.
operations.trigger: A familiar case may illuminate an unfamiliar one.

operations.name: Analogical encoding
operations.definition: Comparing two or more examples to articulate a shared relational schema.
operations.distinction: A training method built around comparison and abstraction.
operations.trigger: You want to learn a principle that transfers across contexts.

operations.name: Pattern recognition
operations.definition: Detecting recurring configurations or regularities in observations.
operations.distinction: Recognition alone does not establish cause.
operations.trigger: Similar arrangements keep appearing.

operations.name: Generalization
operations.definition: Extending a claim or principle across a broader class of cases.
operations.distinction: Abstraction can support generalization, but they are not identical.
operations.trigger: You want to know what carries beyond the observed example.

operations.name: Synthesis
operations.definition: Combining distinct elements or findings into a coherent new whole.
operations.distinction: Decomposition separates; synthesis integrates.
operations.trigger: Several partial insights must work together.

operations.name: Evaluation
operations.definition: Judging something against explicit criteria and evidence.
operations.distinction: Diagnosis asks what caused a problem; evaluation asks how well something meets criteria.
operations.trigger: You must compare quality, fitness, or adequacy.

operations.name: Problem reformulation
operations.definition: Changing the representation or wording of the problem to redirect inquiry.
operations.distinction: Diagnosis can follow reformulation, but reframing changes the question itself.
operations.trigger: Repeated solutions fail, assumptions constrain options, or the question seems misplaced.

operations.name: Extraction
operations.definition: Retrieving or isolating identifiable information from a source.
operations.distinction: Abstraction constructs a selective representation.
operations.trigger: You need specific existing facts or statements.

operations.name: Conceptual delineation
operations.definition: Establishing the boundaries, criteria, and distinctions of a concept.
operations.distinction: Classification applies categories; delineation defines their boundaries.
operations.trigger: Terms overlap or category membership is ambiguous.

operations.name: Classification
operations.definition: Assigning items to categories according to criteria.
operations.distinction: Delineation establishes the category rules.
operations.trigger: You need to organize cases into known classes.

operations.name: Constraint identification
operations.definition: Finding the conditions that limit or govern viable choices.
operations.distinction: Evaluation judges options within those constraints.
operations.trigger: A proposed action may be infeasible or restricted.

operations.name: Metacognitive monitoring
operations.definition: Observing and assessing the quality, progress, and limitations of your own thinking.
operations.distinction: Monitoring notices; regulation changes course.
operations.trigger: You notice uncertainty, drift, repetition, or weak evidence.

operations.name: Metacognitive regulation
operations.definition: Adjusting strategy, effort, representation, or operation in response to monitoring.
operations.distinction: Can include stopping, switching, revisiting, or sequencing.
operations.trigger: Progress stalls or evidence suggests a better approach.

operations.name: Concrete fading
operations.definition: Gradually reducing concrete supports while preserving understanding of a general relationship.
operations.distinction: A learning procedure, not a synonym for abstraction itself.
operations.trigger: You understand examples but struggle to transfer without them.

operations.name: Structural analysis
operations.definition: Examine components, arrangement, boundaries, and how parts fit together.
operations.distinction: Unlike functional analysis, this focuses on arrangement rather than what parts accomplish.
operations.trigger: A program has unclear responsibilities.

operations.name: Functional analysis
operations.definition: Examine what each component does and the contribution it makes to the whole.
operations.distinction: Structural analysis asks how parts are arranged; functional analysis asks what they do.
operations.trigger: The role of parts is unclear.

operations.name: Relational analysis
operations.definition: Examine relationships among entities, including direction, strength, reciprocity, and dependency.
operations.distinction: Structural analysis may show arrangement; relational analysis interrogates the links.
operations.trigger: Connections matter more than isolated elements.

operations.name: Comparative analysis
operations.definition: Systematically compare cases using the same meaningful dimensions.
operations.distinction: Evaluation adds a judgment against criteria; comparison may remain descriptive.
operations.trigger: You need to understand similarities and differences.

operations.name: Gap analysis
operations.definition: Compare a current state with a defined desired state and identify the differences that matter.
operations.distinction: Diagnosis asks why a failure occurs; gap analysis identifies the distance from a target.
operations.trigger: There is a target and uncertainty about what is missing.

operations.name: Root-cause analysis
operations.definition: Investigate the deeper contributing conditions that generate an observed problem.
operations.distinction: Diagnosis identifies a problem cause; root-cause analysis emphasizes upstream drivers and contributing conditions.
operations.trigger: A symptom persists despite local fixes.

operations.name: Mechanistic analysis
operations.definition: Explain an outcome by specifying entities, activities, and interactions that produce it.
operations.distinction: Causal analysis may identify influence; mechanistic analysis explains the producing process.
operations.trigger: A claim says something works without showing how.

operations.name: Systems analysis
operations.definition: Examine interacting components, boundaries, inputs, outputs, feedback, and emergent behavior.
operations.distinction: Decomposition isolates parts; systems analysis also examines their interactions.
operations.trigger: Local explanations miss interactions across a whole.

operations.name: Constraint analysis
operations.definition: Identify limiting conditions and how they shape feasible actions.
operations.distinction: Evaluation judges options; constraint analysis defines the feasible space.
operations.trigger: A plan must operate under restrictions.

operations.name: Assumption analysis
operations.definition: Identify claims being treated as true, assess their support, and test their consequences.
operations.distinction: Inference derives claims; assumption analysis interrogates their starting premises.
operations.trigger: A proposal rests on unstated beliefs.

operations.name: Stakeholder analysis
operations.definition: Examine relevant actors, their interests, influence, incentives, and relationships.
operations.distinction: Relational analysis is broader; stakeholder analysis centers actors and their interests.
operations.trigger: Decisions depend on multiple people or groups.

operations.name: Counterfactual reasoning
operations.definition: Explore what would plausibly change if a condition had been different.
operations.distinction: Prediction looks forward; counterfactual reasoning changes an assumed past or condition.
operations.trigger: You want to test causal significance or alternative pathways.

operations.name: Scenario analysis
operations.definition: Construct plausible future conditions and examine implications across them.
operations.distinction: Counterfactual reasoning changes a condition; scenario analysis compares plausible futures.
operations.trigger: The future is uncertain and plans need robustness.

operations.name: Conceptual analysis
operations.definition: Clarify a concept by examining its meaning, components, relations, and use conditions.
operations.distinction: Conceptual delineation emphasizes boundaries; conceptual analysis can examine the whole idea.
operations.trigger: A key idea is underspecified.

operations.name: Conceptual differentiation
operations.definition: Identify meaningful differences between concepts that seem similar.
operations.distinction: Delineation specifies boundaries; differentiation focuses on contrasts.
operations.trigger: Two terms are being conflated.

operations.name: Taxonomy construction
operations.definition: Design a coherent system of categories and their relationships.
operations.distinction: Classification uses an existing taxonomy; taxonomy construction creates one.
operations.trigger: A domain lacks stable classification structure.

operations.name: Prioritization
operations.definition: Order alternatives by explicit importance, urgency, value, or other criteria.
operations.distinction: Evaluation judges fitness; prioritization adds an ordering for action.
operations.trigger: Resources require sequencing.

operations.name: Operationalization
operations.definition: Translate an abstract concept into observable indicators, measures, or procedures.
operations.distinction: Abstraction builds a conceptual representation; operationalization makes it observable or actionable.
operations.trigger: A concept must be tested or applied.

operations.name: Hypothesis testing
operations.definition: Compare a testable claim against observations capable of supporting or challenging it.
operations.distinction: Abduction proposes hypotheses; testing checks them.
operations.trigger: You have a specific explanation to examine.

operations.name: Evidence appraisal
operations.definition: Assess the relevance, credibility, sufficiency, and limitations of evidence.
operations.distinction: Evaluation is broad; evidence appraisal focuses on support for claims.
operations.trigger: A conclusion depends on uncertain sources.

operations.name: Causal mapping
operations.definition: Represent hypothesized causal influences among variables and inspect pathways.
operations.distinction: Causal analysis is reasoning; causal mapping is a representational technique.
operations.trigger: Multiple causes and feedback may interact.

operations.name: Recontextualization
operations.definition: Place an idea in a different context to examine how its meaning or usefulness changes.
operations.distinction: Analogy maps relationships; recontextualization changes the setting of application.
operations.trigger: A concept may apply beyond its original setting.

operations.name: Reframing
operations.definition: Change the interpretive perspective used to understand a situation.
operations.distinction: Problem reformulation changes the question; reframing may change the interpretive lens without rewriting it.
operations.trigger: An existing perspective narrows possible interpretations.

operations.name: Model building
operations.definition: Construct a simplified conceptual or formal account of entities and relationships to reason with.
operations.distinction: Abstraction is a broader operation; model building produces a specific representation.
operations.trigger: A complex idea needs a coherent representation.

operations.name: Trade-off analysis
operations.definition: Examine gains, losses, and tensions among competing objectives.
operations.distinction: Prioritization orders choices; trade-off analysis exposes their competing consequences.
operations.trigger: Improving one objective may weaken another.

operations.name: Sensitivity analysis
operations.definition: Examine how conclusions or outputs change when assumptions or inputs vary.
operations.distinction: Scenario analysis compares futures; sensitivity analysis isolates dependence on inputs.
operations.trigger: A result may depend heavily on uncertain inputs.

operations.name: Boundary analysis
operations.definition: Examine what is included or excluded from a system, concept, or investigation.
operations.distinction: Conceptual delineation defines a term; boundary analysis may define a system or inquiry scope.
operations.trigger: Scope is unclear or outcomes change with boundaries.

objects.name: Term of art
objects.definition: A specialized term whose meaning is defined by a discipline or practice.
objects.distinction: A term of art is an expression with a specific meaning inside a discipline, even if its everyday meaning differs. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.
objects.trigger: Clarify what a technical term means in context.

objects.name: Mechanism
objects.definition: A process or interaction through which a result is produced.
objects.distinction: A mechanism explains **how** a result comes about through connected steps or interactions. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Phenomenon
objects.definition: An observable occurrence or pattern requiring description or explanation.
objects.distinction: A phenomenon is something that happens or is observed and calls for description or explanation. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Principle
objects.definition: A general guiding rule or relationship used across cases.
objects.distinction: A principle is a general statement that guides reasoning or action across cases. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Process / workflow
objects.definition: A sequence of activities and transitions producing an outcome.
objects.distinction: A process is an ordered set of activities that changes an input into an outcome. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Structure / architecture
objects.definition: The arrangement and relationships of parts in a whole.
objects.distinction: Structure describes how parts are arranged and related. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Relationship / dependency
objects.definition: A connection in which entities influence, require, or constrain one another.
objects.distinction: A relationship connects two or more things; a dependency is a relationship in which one thing relies on another. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Pattern
objects.definition: A recurring configuration across cases or time.
objects.distinction: A pattern is a recognizable recurrence in how events, features, or relationships are arranged. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Model / framework
objects.definition: A simplified representation or organizing system for understanding or action.
objects.distinction: A model selectively represents how something works or is organized; a framework supplies a structure for organizing thought or action. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Method / technique
objects.definition: A repeatable way of performing an activity.
objects.distinction: A method is a repeatable approach for achieving an objective; a technique is a specific procedure used within or alongside that approach. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.
objects.trigger: Evaluate or improve how work is done.

objects.name: Effect / outcome
objects.definition: A result or consequence of activities and conditions.
objects.distinction: An effect is a change produced or influenced by something else. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Constraint / governing condition
objects.definition: A limit or condition that shapes what can happen or be chosen.
objects.distinction: A constraint limits which actions or explanations are possible. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Hypothesis
objects.definition: A provisional, potentially testable claim or explanation.
objects.distinction: A hypothesis is a provisional claim you can examine against evidence. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Assumption
objects.definition: A premise accepted provisionally, sometimes without direct verification.
objects.distinction: An assumption is something taken as true for the purpose of reasoning, even if it has not yet been established. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Concept / idea
objects.definition: A mental category or construct used to organize meaning.
objects.distinction: A concept is a mental category or organized idea that helps you recognize and reason about something. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

objects.name: Decision / judgment
objects.definition: A selection or assessment based on information and criteria.
objects.distinction: A decision is a choice among possible actions. The object is what you investigate; the operation is the thinking you do to it.

outputs.name: Comparison matrix
outputs.definition: Rows represent items; columns represent consistent dimensions; cells contain comparable evidence.
outputs.distinction: A timeline emphasizes sequence rather than comparison.

outputs.name: Evidence matrix
outputs.definition: Rows represent claims or hypotheses; columns represent evidence sources; cells record support, contradiction, or uncertainty.
outputs.distinction: A concept map does not systematically score evidence.
outputs.trigger: Compare several hypotheses against several observations.

outputs.name: Decision matrix
outputs.definition: Alternatives are rows; criteria are columns; scores or judgments express performance, optionally weighted.
outputs.distinction: A comparison matrix may remain descriptive without deciding.
outputs.trigger: Choose among options with explicit criteria.

outputs.name: Synthesis matrix
outputs.definition: Rows group sources or themes; columns capture shared questions; cells hold distilled findings; final synthesis crosses rows.
outputs.distinction: A source inventory merely lists materials.
outputs.trigger: Integrate findings across sources or themes.

outputs.name: Concept map
outputs.definition: Nodes are concepts; labeled links state semantic relationships; layout is non-sequential.
outputs.distinction: A flowchart represents decisions or process flow.

outputs.name: Causal diagram
outputs.definition: Variables or factors connect through directional causal arrows; label polarity or assumptions when useful.
outputs.distinction: A concept map may express noncausal relations.

outputs.name: Causal loop diagram
outputs.definition: Variables connect in directed loops; mark reinforcing or balancing feedback and delays where relevant.
outputs.distinction: A linear flowchart does not represent feedback dynamics well.

outputs.name: Process flowchart
outputs.definition: Actions and decision diamonds connect with directional arrows and branches.
outputs.distinction: A cycle shows recurrence but usually lacks detailed branching.
outputs.trigger: Represent how a workflow proceeds and branches.

outputs.name: Cycle diagram
outputs.definition: Stages connect in a closed repeating sequence.
outputs.distinction: A process flowchart can include branches and terminal states.

outputs.name: Flywheel
outputs.definition: A reinforcing cycle highlights how each stage strengthens the next and accumulates momentum.
outputs.distinction: A cycle can repeat without compounding.

outputs.name: Timeline
outputs.definition: Events are positioned along a time axis, preserving order and optionally intervals.
outputs.distinction: A stage model abstracts phases rather than precise dates.

outputs.name: Stage model
outputs.definition: Distinct phases are ordered by developmental or functional transitions, not necessarily fixed dates.
outputs.distinction: A timeline depicts chronological events.
outputs.trigger: Explain how something develops through phases.

outputs.name: Decision tree
outputs.definition: Branches represent choices or chance events; endpoints represent consequences or classifications.
outputs.distinction: A taxonomy organizes categories without choice paths.

outputs.name: Taxonomy
outputs.definition: Categories are organized by defined class membership and parent–child relations.
outputs.distinction: A concept map allows many types of links, not just class relations.

outputs.name: Hierarchy diagram
outputs.definition: Nodes arranged in levels show rank, authority, or containment, with labeled relation type.
outputs.distinction: A taxonomy specifically classifies types.

outputs.name: Systems map
outputs.definition: Elements, boundaries, and labeled relationships show interacting parts of a system.
outputs.distinction: A process flowchart emphasizes step sequence.

outputs.name: Dependency graph
outputs.definition: Directed edges indicate that one element requires or enables another.
outputs.distinction: A hierarchy need not show dependencies.

outputs.name: Stakeholder map
outputs.definition: Actors are positioned by influence, interest, or relationship; links show interactions.
outputs.distinction: A systems map may include nonhuman components.

outputs.name: Argument map
outputs.definition: Claims connect to supporting reasons, objections, and evidence through labeled links.
outputs.distinction: A concept map need not distinguish evidential support.
outputs.trigger: Evaluate or communicate the structure of an argument.

outputs.name: Logic model
outputs.definition: Inputs → activities → outputs → short- and long-term outcomes, with assumptions.
outputs.distinction: A process flowchart focuses on execution steps.
outputs.trigger: Explain how a program is expected to produce results.

outputs.name: Framework
outputs.definition: An organized set of concepts, dimensions, or principles used to guide analysis or action.
outputs.distinction: A model more specifically represents how a phenomenon works.
outputs.trigger: Give repeatable structure to decisions or investigation.

outputs.name: Conceptual model
outputs.definition: A simplified set of concepts and hypothesized relations explaining or organizing a phenomenon.
outputs.distinction: A framework may guide work without explaining relationships.

outputs.name: Rubric
outputs.definition: Criteria and performance levels describe what quality looks like.
outputs.distinction: A decision matrix compares alternatives; a rubric describes standards.

outputs.name: Checklist
outputs.definition: A finite set of conditions or steps to verify, usually with binary completion states.
outputs.distinction: A rubric judges degrees of quality rather than completion.

outputs.name: Narrative synthesis
outputs.definition: A coherent prose account that integrates findings into an interpreted explanation or argument, showing how they connect and what they mean.
outputs.distinction: A summary condenses sources; a narrative synthesis integrates and interprets them. A timeline orders events; a narrative synthesis need not be chronological. The cognitive operation is synthesis; “narrative” specifies the representation.
outputs.trigger: Many pieces of evidence need an integrated, readable explanation of the relationships and implications.

outputs.name: Analytical brief
outputs.definition: A concise, decision-oriented written analysis that foregrounds the question, evidence, implications, and recommendation.
outputs.distinction: A narrative synthesis prioritizes coherent integration of evidence; an analytical brief prioritizes a decision under constraints.
outputs.trigger: A stakeholder needs a short, reasoned account that supports a concrete choice.

outputs.name: Trade-off matrix
outputs.definition: A table that makes competing benefits, costs, and sacrifices explicit across possible choices.
outputs.distinction: A decision matrix often assigns weights or scores to choose a winner; a trade-off matrix first makes the competing sacrifices explicit without requiring a numerical ranking.
outputs.trigger: Each option improves some criteria but worsens others.

outputs.name: Typology
outputs.definition: A structured set of meaningful types based on chosen distinguishing characteristics.
outputs.distinction: A taxonomy usually emphasizes systematic classification, often hierarchical; a typology emphasizes analytically useful types and their defining dimensions.
outputs.trigger: A broad category contains several recurring subtypes that require different interpretations or responses.

outputs.name: Worked example
outputs.definition: A concrete, step-by-step demonstration of how a method or cognitive operation is performed on a specific case.
outputs.distinction: An example only illustrates a concept; a worked example exposes the process of applying it.
outputs.trigger: You know a definition but cannot yet picture the steps or decision points involved.

lenses.name: Causal
lenses.definition: Focus on influence, contributing conditions, and cause–effect pathways.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when the question asks why something happens or what change might produce an effect.

lenses.name: Structural
lenses.definition: Focus on components, arrangement, interfaces, and boundaries.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when organization, configuration, or boundaries may explain the situation.

lenses.name: Functional
lenses.definition: Focus on roles, purposes, and contributions of parts.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when you need to understand roles, purposes, or contributions.

lenses.name: Temporal
lenses.definition: Focus on sequence, duration, transitions, and change over time.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when sequence, timing, stages, or change over time matter.

lenses.name: Relational
lenses.definition: Focus on connections, dependencies, and interactions.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when the important information lies between the parts.

lenses.name: Hierarchical
lenses.definition: Focus on levels, authority, nesting, and class relations.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when parent–child structure, authority, or levels of generality matter.

lenses.name: Mechanistic
lenses.definition: Focus on producing activities and interactions that generate an effect.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when the chain of production matters; do not force it onto a purely descriptive task.

lenses.name: Comparative
lenses.definition: Focus on differences and similarities along consistent dimensions.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when you must distinguish alternatives or detect shared properties.

lenses.name: Systemic
lenses.definition: Focus on interdependence, feedback, boundaries, and emergent effects.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when local changes have wider or recurring consequences.

lenses.name: Behavioral
lenses.definition: Focus on observable actions, incentives, habits, and decisions.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when choices, habits, incentives, or actions are central.

lenses.name: Epistemic
lenses.definition: Focus on knowledge claims, evidence, uncertainty, and justification.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when confidence, evidence quality, or knowledge limits determine the next step.

lenses.name: Normative
lenses.definition: Focus on what ought to be done under explicit values or standards.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when evaluating legitimacy, fairness, duties, or desired standards.

lenses.name: Micro level
lenses.definition: Focus on individual elements or local interactions.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when local actions, elements, or interactions require close examination.

lenses.name: Meso level
lenses.definition: Focus on relationships and mechanisms connecting local and whole-system levels.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when handoffs, group dynamics, or inter-unit mechanisms are the missing link.

lenses.name: Macro level
lenses.definition: Focus on the system or large-scale arrangement.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when the overall configuration, direction, or population-level pattern matters.

lenses.name: Meta level
lenses.definition: Focus on governing rules, assumptions, and the way the inquiry itself is organized.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when the thinking process, evaluation rules, or governing framework needs examination.

lenses.name: Scope
lenses.definition: Limit the investigation to defined actors, times, boundaries, or questions.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when a question is too broad, underspecified, or likely to drift.

lenses.name: Criteria
lenses.definition: Specify standards used to judge adequacy or quality.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when judgments or choices need explicit standards.

lenses.name: Constraints
lenses.definition: Specify hard limits or governing conditions for feasible answers.
lenses.distinction: A lens changes what you attend to; an operation specifies the mental transformation. A level specifies scale, not a particular operation.
lenses.trigger: Use when options must remain within stated limits.
